Overview and Clinical Burden of Craniofacial Bone Defects

Craniofacial bone defects arise from congenital anomalies, traumatic injuries (including high-energy and blast mechanisms), infections, and oncologic resections of locally aggressive tumors, and they impose substantial functional, aesthetic, and economic burdens. <cite id="b06d4076-0">Large craniomaxillofacial defects can result from high-energy impact, blast injuries, congenital defects, and tumor resection; many are “critical-sized” and cannot heal spontaneously, requiring surgical reconstruction</cite>. <cite id="b06d4076-2">Trauma is a leading global cause of death in children, and pediatric facial fractures commonly involve the head/face, with notable case fatality rates; craniofacial defects from trauma or oncologic resection disrupt bone and soft tissues and resist spontaneous healing</cite>. <cite id="b06d4076-0">In the U.S., more than 400,000 patients present annually with facial fractures or large craniofacial defects at over $1 billion in cost, and incidence trends continue upward</cite>. <cite id="b06d4076-2">Reconstruction is difficult because craniofacial defects span multiple tissue types and structures, and nonhealing composite wounds reflect mismatched soft-tissue and bone deficits</cite>.

Functionally, craniofacial bone supports mastication, speech articulation, airway patency, and facial contour; deficits jeopardize these domains and have psychosocial sequelae. <cite id="c56c238d-0">Craniofacial bone defects impair mastication, pronunciation, and facial appearance</cite>. <cite id="c56c238d-1">The mandible anchors masticatory muscles and contributes to speech and breathing; segmental resection is performed for advanced oral cavity malignancies and necessitates reconstruction to restore airway patency, speech, facial contour, and oral intake</cite>. <cite id="b06d4076-4">In children, inadequately treated craniofacial fractures risk long-term functional impairment, facial asymmetry, growth disturbances, and psychosocial sequelae, reflecting the unique growth and remodeling capacities of pediatric craniofacial bone</cite>. <cite id="b06d4076-0">Clinically, these defects demand three-dimensional structural support, including protection of brain tissue, mechanical stability for jaw movement, and high aesthetic quality, making them both biomedically and economically burdensome</cite>.

Critical-Sized Bone Defects (CSBDs): Definition, Thresholds, and Pathophysiology

A critical-sized bone defect (CSBD) is a size and complexity of injury that will not heal spontaneously to regenerate bone and restore function without surgical intervention. <cite id="78468f3e-0">Critical-size bone defects are defined as defects too large to heal spontaneously during a patient’s lifetime without surgical intervention</cite>. <cite id="78468f3e-1">There is no agreed universal definition in humans; Court-Brown defined a defect involving 50% of cortical diameter with a minimum length of 1 cm as critical in tibia, and in settings with fracture-related infection, such definitions inform treatment strategies even as healing without surgery occurs in a substantial fraction</cite>. <cite id="b06d4076-0">In the craniomaxillofacial region, many large defects are considered critical and require planned reconstruction to heal</cite>.

The 5 mm threshold originates largely from experimental models and is anatomical-site–specific. <cite id="78468f3e-2">Schmitz and Hollinger defined CSBDs as the smallest intraosseous wound in a given bone and species that will not heal spontaneously; in rodent calvaria, defects exceeding about 5.0 mm have been labeled critical, though with high heterogeneity across studies, whereas in dogs ~20 mm represented a critical threshold, and in humans no clearly defined CSBD value exists due to ethical constraints and differences in bone structure and regenerative capacity</cite>. <cite id="78468f3e-2">Although a human calvarial defect exceeding 2–2.5 cm is often considered nonhealing, these values lack high-level confirmatory evidence</cite>. In practice, clinicians infer criticality when defects exceed the capacity of endogenous healing mechanisms to restore bone continuity and stability, often requiring structural grafts or osteoinductive/osteogenic augmentation.

Healing barriers in CSBDs are mechanistic and interdependent: initial avascularity and poor integration of osteogenic cells lead to cell death and fibrous connective tissue rather than bone. <cite id="c56c238d-0">The defect area is initially avascular, and introduced osteogenic cells die without timely vascularization, so strategies must concurrently promote osteogenesis and vasculogenesis, including angiogenic growth factors and cell-based vascularization; scaffold surface morphology and porosity guide cell behavior and neovascularization</cite>. <cite id="c56c238d-2">Craniofacial bone is highly dependent on an unobstructed vascular network for cell proliferation and waste removal; after injury, recruited osteogenic cells (e.g., primary osteoblasts, pluripotent stem cells) fail if vasculogenesis does not establish rapidly, producing failed regeneration</cite>. <cite id="78468f3e-3">A consensus in bone tissue engineering is that effective regeneration requires a biomimetic scaffold, cells and growth factors to attract desired cell types, and an emergent vasculature to support tissue survival beyond a certain size</cite>. These mechanisms explain why CSBDs risk nonunion or formation of a fibrous/hyaline scar that fails to provide the structural, mechanical, and biological continuity of native bone.

Clinical and Oncologic Context in Craniofacial Care

Craniofacial CSBDs frequently arise from high-impact trauma and oncologic resections, demanding multidisciplinary reconstruction to preserve function and aesthetics. <cite id="b06d4076-0">High-energy trauma and tumor resections are prominent causes of large craniomaxillofacial defects that require planned, reconstructive surgery</cite>. <cite id="b06d4076-3">Large defects from trauma, tumor resection, congenital anomalies, infection, and revision surgery remain unresolved challenges in orthopedic, maxillofacial, and reconstructive surgery</cite>. <cite id="c56c238d-3">Oral and maxillofacial defects after tumor resection are commonly classified by site (oral cavity, mandible, maxilla, midface) and by soft- or hard-tissue involvement; correct classification guides reconstruction and improves outcomes by aligning techniques with speech, swallowing, and aesthetic goals</cite>.

Mandibular oncologic defects illustrate the complexity and functional stakes. <cite id="c56c238d-1">Segmental mandibulectomy is required for advanced oral cavity malignancies and is also used for osteonecrosis; reconstruction restores airway patency, speech, facial contour, and oral intake, with strategies ranging from microvascular free flaps to dental rehabilitation</cite>. <cite id="c56c238d-4">Reconstruction frequently employs vascularized microvascular free flaps (e.g., fibula) or autogenous bone grafts, but these cannot fully replicate the mandible’s geometry and function, and reconstructions often encounter functional deficits despite advances</cite>. <cite id="c56c238d-4">Oromandibular reconstruction is challenged by tumor resection, osteomyelitis, and osteoradionecrosis, requiring multidisciplinary planning to recover width, height, and projection of the facial dimensions</cite>. <cite id="b06d4076-2">War-related and other mass casualty settings have demonstrated the scale and complexity of craniofacial reconstruction, with international teams deploying composite and oral rehabilitation techniques to restore function and appearance</cite>.

Implications for Management: From Thresholds to Therapeutic Strategies

Clinically, the 5 mm (model-derived) and site-specific critical-size concepts guide whether conservative, osteoconductive, osteoinductive, or osteogenic strategies are required. <cite id="78468f3e-2">Rodent calvarial “critical” thresholds near 5 mm underscore how healing capacity is anatomical-site–dependent and that human thresholds are not directly transferable from animal models</cite>. <cite id="78468f3e-1">Where infection coexists with segmental bone loss, criticality increases and treatment strategies (Ilizarov, Papineau, Masquelet, RIA) show wide success variability, reinforcing that biological milieu and soft-tissue viability shape outcomes</cite>. <cite id="c56c238d-0">Because defects are initially avascular, successful craniofacial bone regeneration requires integrating vasculogenesis with osteogenesis, using angiogenic factors, prevascularized or vascularized constructs, and scaffolds that guide cell behavior</cite>. <cite id="78468f3e-3">A unifying framework emphasizes scaffolds, cells/growth factors, and engineered vasculature to sustain tissue survival as constructs exceed critical size</cite>.

Practically, this translates into choosing interventions that bridge the gap between nonhealing CSBDs and functional restoration. <cite id="c56c238d-2">Autologous/allogeneic bone grafts remain gold standards but carry donor-site morbidity, infection risk, and challenges establishing deep vasculogenesis, leading to graft necrosis; new strategies target neovascular networks to improve integration</cite>. <cite id="b06d4076-0">Reconstruction must provide temporary structural support while restoring neuroprotection, mechanics for jaw motion, facial esthetics, and faster healing</cite>. <cite id="c56c238d-1">In oncologic reconstructions such as segmental mandibulectomy, microvascular composite free flaps and timely implant placement restore airway, speech, contour, and mastication, highlighting the coupling of hard- and soft-tissue healing</cite>.

Key Takeaways

- Etiologies and burden: Craniofacial bone defects from congenital, traumatic, and oncologic causes impose major functional, cosmetic, and economic burdens, demanding multidisciplinary, site-specific reconstruction. <cite id="b06d4076-0">Large craniomaxillofacial defects are often critical and require surgical reconstruction</cite>; <cite id="b06d4076-2">trauma and oncologic resection are major drivers</cite>; <cite id="b06d4076-0">annual U.S. presentations exceed 400,000 with >$1B cost</cite>; <cite id="c56c238d-0">defects impair mastication, speech, and aesthetics</cite>.
- CSBD definition and thresholds: <cite id="78468f3e-0">CSBDs are defects that won’t heal without surgery</cite>; <cite id="78468f3e-1">no universal human definition exists, though 50% cortical loss with 1 cm length has been used in tibia</cite>; <cite id="78468f3e-2">rodent calvarial ~5 mm and human calvarial >2–2.5 cm are commonly cited, but human evidence is limited and site-specific</cite>.
- Mechanisms: <cite id="c56c238d-0">Initial avascularity kills recruited osteogenic cells; regeneration needs concurrent vasculogenesis with osteogenesis</cite>; <cite id="78468f3e-3">scaffolds, cells/growth factors, and engineered vasculature are required to sustain tissue survival beyond a size threshold</cite>.
- Oncologic/functional complexity: <cite id="c56c238d-1">Segmental mandibulectomy exemplifies the need to restore airway, speech, contour, and mastication via microvascular reconstructions and dental rehabilitation</cite>; <cite id="c56c238d-4">current gold standards face limitations in replicating complex mandibular geometry and function, underscoring unmet needs</cite>.

Remaining uncertainties and clinical translation gaps include whether a precise human calvarial “5 mm” rule applies, how infection and radiation compromise criticality, and how to reliably engineer prevascularized constructs that integrate in complex craniofacial sites. <cite id="78468f3e-2">Extrapolating animal thresholds to humans is cautioned due to differences in bone architecture and regenerative capacity</cite>, and <cite id="c56c238d-2">donor-site morbidity, infection, and deep vascularization failure remain key risks of current grafts</cite>. Ongoing advances in biomaterials, prevascularized scaffolds, and combined osteogenic/angiogenic strategies aim to restore the intertwined needs for blood supply and bone continuity that define CSBD care. <cite id="c56c238d-0">Reconstruction strategies now explicitly couple osteogenesis with vasculogenesis, using angiogenic factors and cell-based vascularization, and engineering scaffold topography to direct cell behavior</cite>. <cite id="78468f3e-3">This integrative view—cells, growth factors, biomimetic structure, and engineered vasculature—frames the next wave of critical-size craniofacial bone defect repair</cite>.

Snippet: Segmental bone loss after trauma remains a challenging problem for orthopedic trauma surgeons. When a bone defect exists combined with fracture-related infection (FRI), the chances of successful bone consolidation and clearance of infection are reduced.

There is no agreed definition of what constitutes a critical defect in humans. Court-Brown defined it [1] as a defect involving 50% of the cortical diameter with a minimum length of 1 cm, and this was used in the Study to Prospectively evaluate Intramedullary Nails in Tibial fractures (SPRINT) [2]. A study by Sanders et al. [3] showed that, when using this definition, 47% of the bone defects healed without additional surgery, thus indicating that these are not always critical defects. Over the past decades, critical-sized bone defects in FRI have been treated using different protocols. Techniques used (e.g., Ilizarov, Papineau, Masquelet, or RIA) all have different indications and success rates, resulting in a wide range of clinical outcomes. The concept of critical-size defects (CSDs) is a fundamental issue related to cranial bone repair and regeneration. Schmitz and Hollinger initially defined it as the smallest intraosseous wound in a particular bone and species of animal that will not heal spontaneously during its lifetime [30]. Currently, it is understood as a cranial defect that cannot be healed without surgical intervention, with a variable size depending on the anatomical location and individual patient-related factors. A recent meta-analysis on rodent models suggested that a calvarial defect exceeding 5.0 mm should be considered a CSD; however, the heterogeneity of the included studies was high [40]. In dogs, 20.0 mm was considered the critical threshold [30]. In humans, there is no clearly defined CSD value, as a study to properly evaluate it would likely breach numerous ethical recommendations. In addition, extrapolation from animal models is not recommended, as the bone structure and capacity for bone regeneration differ significantly [41]. Although a human calvarial defect exceeding 2-2.5 cm is considered incapable of spontaneous healing, these values have not been proven through a high-level scientific approach [42][43][44]. The unique anatomical features of the cranial bone structure present specific challenges for regenerative approaches, which differ significantly from long bone repair. The human cranium contains 22 bones, divided primarily into two main regions: the neurocranium, which protects the brain and sensory organs, and the viscerocranium, which supports the facial structure. This complex architecture encompasses bones with distinct developmental origins, healing characteristics, vascularization, thicknesses, and ratios of cortical versus porous bone, among other features [45]. Cranial bone formation is driven by two distinct ossification processes. The cranial base is primarily formed through endochondral ossification, resulting in a more compact, dense, and less flexible structure.

Snippet: Craniofacial bone defects are usually secondary to accident trauma, resection of tumor, sever inflammation, and congenital disease. The defects of craniofacial bones impact esthetic appearance and functionality such as mastication, pronunciation, and facial features. During the craniofacial bone regeneration process, different osteogenic cells are introduced, including primary osteoblasts or pluripotent stem cells. However, the defect area is initially avascular, resulting in the death of the introduced cells and failed regeneration. Thus, it is vital to establish vascularization strategies to build a timely and abundant blood vessel supply network. This review paper therefore focuses on the reconstruction of both osteogenesis and vasculogenesis. The current challenges, various strategies, and latest efforts applied to enhance vascularization in craniofacial bone regeneration are discussed. These involve the application of angiogenic growth factors and cell-based vascularization strategies. In addition, surface morphology, porous characters, and the angiogenic release property of scaffolds also have a fundamental effect on vasculogenesis via cell behavior and are further discussed.
</snippet>

Title: Mandibular rehabilitation: From the Andy Gump deformity to jaw‐in‐a‐day
Snippet: The mandible is a critical structure of the lower facial skeleton which plays an important role in several vital functions, including feeding, speech production and breathing. Segmental resection of the mandible is at times required to ensure en bloc tumor removal in patients with advanced oral cavity malignancies. It is less commonly performed for primary tumors of the mandible or for osteonecrosis related to radiation therapy or bisphosphonates. 2][3][4][5] Mandibular reconstruction is warranted to restore airway patency, improve speech articulation, reestablish the lower facial contour, and restore adequate oral intake. 

The latter is particularly challenging given the complex threedimensional anatomy of the mandible. 7][8] Significant advances have been made over the past decade in the ability to reconstruct and rehabilitate patients after a segmental mandibulectomy. This includes composite microvascular free tissue transfer, as well as dental restoration. This review will highlight these advances, evaluate their efficacy, and discuss the timing of dental implantation.
</snippet>
<snippet id=c56c238d-2>
Title: Vascularization Reconstruction Strategies in Craniofacial Bone Regeneration
Snippet: Craniofacial bone provides support for adjacent craniofacial soft tissues (especially the attachments of mastication-related muscles) and anchorage for dental structures [1]. The defects of craniofacial bones, secondary to accident trauma, congenital disease, tumor resection, and inflammation [2][3][4][5], impact esthetic appearance and functionality of the craniofacial complex, such as mastication, pronunciation, and facial features. Furthermore, craniofacial bone is highly vascularized, and its functions depend a lot on an unobstructed and well-organized vascular network. With the intact vessels, sufficient oxygen and nutrients can be supplied, guaranteeing the proliferation and viability of cells [6]. At the same time, the metabolic waste of cells can be taken away [7]. Therefore, it is wellrecognized that the prompting of vasculogenesis is beneficial for reinforced bone functions. After the craniofacial bone defect occurs, osteogenic cells such as primary osteoblasts or pluripotent stem cells are recruited in order to generate neobones. However, the defect area is initially avascular, resulting in the death of the recruited cells and failed regeneration [6]. Thus, it is vital to establish vascularization strategies to build a timely and abundant blood vessel supply network [8]. 

Clinically, the damaged craniofacial bone can be reconstructed with a series of surgical operations. More than 90% of grafts used are autologous or allogenic transplantations, which are recognized as the "gold standards" [9]. However, challenges, such as donor site morbidity, pain, infection, and additional economic burden, are still unmet [10]. More importantly, vasculogenesis in the depth of the defect also cannot be well-established, which leads to the necrosis of transplanted grafts [11][12][13]. 

Coatings 2024, 14, 357 2 of 18 Rapid developments in bone tissue engineering bring new hope for solving the urgent problems and provide more strategies for neovascular networks and craniofacial bone tissue regeneration.
</snippet>
<snippet id=c56c238d-3>
Title: Reconstructive strategies for post-oncological oral and maxillofacial defects: A systematic overview of novel techniques and outcomes
Snippet: Oral and maxillofacial defects caused by resection of tumors are extremely frequently complicated post-oncology defects and affect the strategies of reconstruction. These defects are classified according to their localization in the human body (oral cavity, mandible, maxilla and midface) and lesion of anatomical structure: (a) soft-tissue, (b) hardtissue or (c) composite. Correctly classifying lesions, e.g., the brown system of classifying maxillary defects, enlightens the approach to surgery, considering the functions (speech and swallowing) and aesthetics. Defining the nature of defects is crucial for selecting the most effective method of reconstruction, as it also improves patient outcomes.
</snippet>
<snippet id=c56c238d-4>
Title: The Potential of Magnesium Based Materials in Mandibular Reconstruction
Snippet: The mandible is the largest and the strongest bone in the human face, serving as a support to the oral musculature and thereby aiding in articulation, respiration, deglutition, and mastication. Furthermore, it is crucial in maintaining the facial profile by supporting the skeletal base for teeth [1]. Several issues like tumor resection, congenital defects, and associated trauma needing many reconstructive surgeries in the mandibular zone is one of the routine challenges in clinical practice [2]. One of the potential challenges often encountered by clinicians is the oromandibular reconstruction during episodes of benign/malignant tumor resection, and management of osteomyelitis or the osteoradionecrotic mandible. Mandibular defects often occur due to the surgical therapies for malignant tumors surfacing in the neck and head regions. Often, these defects jeopardize both form and function of the mandible, requiring a multi-disciplinary approach to restore their function and aesthetics. Significant factors to be considered during the reconstruction of such defects include the re-establishment of facial dimensions in terms of their width, height, and projection. Despite the advancements, during the critical assessment of the reconstructed oral cavity, functional deficits are often encountered. Besides radical removal of the tumor, current prospects of maxillofacial surgery demand subsequent primary/secondary reconstruction taking into consideration the patient factors that have an important role in terms of efficient function, aesthetics, and dental rehabilitation. Various surgical methodologies have been adopted for mandibular defect reconstruction that possess unique advantages and limitations. Some of these surgical procedures include free bone graft, reconstruction plate, particulate bone cancellous marrow graft, transport distraction osteogenesis, microvascular free flap, pedicle bone graft, modular endoprosthesis, and tissue engineering. 

The current gold standard treatment modalities for mandibular defect reconstruction includes: (a) vascularized microvascular free fibula flap or (b) an autogenous free bone graft. However, the bone graft treatment possesses certain limitations, such as its inability to replicate the complex geometry of the original mandible. Further, it also lacks in mimicking the aesthetic and function aspect completely like the original.

Overview and Clinical Burden of Craniofacial Bone Defects

Craniofacial bone defects arise from congenital anomalies, traumatic injuries (including high-energy and blast mechanisms), infections, and oncologic resections of locally aggressive tumors, and they impose substantial functional, aesthetic, and economic burdens. <cite id="b06d4076-0">Large craniomaxillofacial defects can result from high-energy impact, blast injuries, congenital defects, and tumor resection; many are “critical-sized” and cannot heal spontaneously, requiring surgical reconstruction</cite>. <cite id="b06d4076-2">Trauma is a leading global cause of death in children, and pediatric facial fractures commonly involve the head/face, with notable case fatality rates; craniofacial defects from trauma or oncologic resection disrupt bone and soft tissues and resist spontaneous healing</cite>. <cite id="b06d4076-0">In the U.S., more than 400,000 patients present annually with facial fractures or large craniofacial defects at over $1 billion in cost, and incidence trends continue upward</cite>. <cite id="b06d4076-2">Reconstruction is difficult because craniofacial defects span multiple tissue types and structures, and nonhealing composite wounds reflect mismatched soft-tissue and bone deficits</cite>.

Functionally, craniofacial bone supports mastication, speech articulation, airway patency, and facial contour; deficits jeopardize these domains and have psychosocial sequelae. <cite id="c56c238d-0">Craniofacial bone defects impair mastication, pronunciation, and facial appearance</cite>. <cite id="c56c238d-1">The mandible anchors masticatory muscles and contributes to speech and breathing; segmental resection is performed for advanced oral cavity malignancies and necessitates reconstruction to restore airway patency, speech, facial contour, and oral intake</cite>. <cite id="b06d4076-4">In children, inadequately treated craniofacial fractures risk long-term functional impairment, facial asymmetry, growth disturbances, and psychosocial sequelae, reflecting the unique growth and remodeling capacities of pediatric craniofacial bone</cite>. <cite id="b06d4076-0">Clinically, these defects demand three-dimensional structural support, including protection of brain tissue, mechanical stability for jaw movement, and high aesthetic quality, making them both biomedically and economically burdensome</cite>.

Critical-Sized Bone Defects (CSBDs): Definition, Thresholds, and Pathophysiology

A critical-sized bone defect (CSBD) is a size and complexity of injury that will not heal spontaneously to regenerate bone and restore function without surgical intervention. <cite id="78468f3e-0">Critical-size bone defects are defined as defects too large to heal spontaneously during a patient’s lifetime without surgical intervention</cite>. <cite id="78468f3e-1">There is no agreed universal definition in humans; Court-Brown defined a defect involving 50% of cortical diameter with a minimum length of 1 cm as critical in tibia, and in settings with fracture-related infection, such definitions inform treatment strategies even as healing without surgery occurs in a substantial fraction</cite>. <cite id="b06d4076-0">In the craniomaxillofacial region, many large defects are considered critical and require planned reconstruction to heal</cite>.

The 5 mm threshold originates largely from experimental models and is anatomical-site–specific. <cite id="78468f3e-2">Schmitz and Hollinger defined CSBDs as the smallest intraosseous wound in a given bone and species that will not heal spontaneously; in rodent calvaria, defects exceeding about 5.0 mm have been labeled critical, though with high heterogeneity across studies, whereas in dogs ~20 mm represented a critical threshold, and in humans no clearly defined CSBD value exists due to ethical constraints and differences in bone structure and regenerative capacity</cite>. <cite id="78468f3e-2">Although a human calvarial defect exceeding 2–2.5 cm is often considered nonhealing, these values lack high-level confirmatory evidence</cite>. In practice, clinicians infer criticality when defects exceed the capacity of endogenous healing mechanisms to restore bone continuity and stability, often requiring structural grafts or osteoinductive/osteogenic augmentation.

Healing barriers in CSBDs are mechanistic and interdependent: initial avascularity and poor integration of osteogenic cells lead to cell death and fibrous connective tissue rather than bone. <cite id="c56c238d-0">The defect area is initially avascular, and introduced osteogenic cells die without timely vascularization, so strategies must concurrently promote osteogenesis and vasculogenesis, including angiogenic growth factors and cell-based vascularization; scaffold surface morphology and porosity guide cell behavior and neovascularization</cite>. <cite id="c56c238d-2">Craniofacial bone is highly dependent on an unobstructed vascular network for cell proliferation and waste removal; after injury, recruited osteogenic cells (e.g., primary osteoblasts, pluripotent stem cells) fail if vasculogenesis does not establish rapidly, producing failed regeneration</cite>. <cite id="78468f3e-3">A consensus in bone tissue engineering is that effective regeneration requires a biomimetic scaffold, cells and growth factors to attract desired cell types, and an emergent vasculature to support tissue survival beyond a certain size</cite>. These mechanisms explain why CSBDs risk nonunion or formation of a fibrous/hyaline scar that fails to provide the structural, mechanical, and biological continuity of native bone.

Clinical and Oncologic Context in Craniofacial Care

Craniofacial CSBDs frequently arise from high-impact trauma and oncologic resections, demanding multidisciplinary reconstruction to preserve function and aesthetics. <cite id="b06d4076-0">High-energy trauma and tumor resections are prominent causes of large craniomaxillofacial defects that require planned, reconstructive surgery</cite>. <cite id="b06d4076-3">Large defects from trauma, tumor resection, congenital anomalies, infection, and revision surgery remain unresolved challenges in orthopedic, maxillofacial, and reconstructive surgery</cite>. <cite id="c56c238d-3">Oral and maxillofacial defects after tumor resection are commonly classified by site (oral cavity, mandible, maxilla, midface) and by soft- or hard-tissue involvement; correct classification guides reconstruction and improves outcomes by aligning techniques with speech, swallowing, and aesthetic goals</cite>.

Mandibular oncologic defects illustrate the complexity and functional stakes. <cite id="c56c238d-1">Segmental mandibulectomy is required for advanced oral cavity malignancies and is also used for osteonecrosis; reconstruction restores airway patency, speech, facial contour, and oral intake, with strategies ranging from microvascular free flaps to dental rehabilitation</cite>. <cite id="c56c238d-4">Reconstruction frequently employs vascularized microvascular free flaps (e.g., fibula) or autogenous bone grafts, but these cannot fully replicate the mandible’s geometry and function, and reconstructions often encounter functional deficits despite advances</cite>. <cite id="c56c238d-4">Oromandibular reconstruction is challenged by tumor resection, osteomyelitis, and osteoradionecrosis, requiring multidisciplinary planning to recover width, height, and projection of the facial dimensions</cite>. <cite id="b06d4076-2">War-related and other mass casualty settings have demonstrated the scale and complexity of craniofacial reconstruction, with international teams deploying composite and oral rehabilitation techniques to restore function and appearance</cite>.

Implications for Management: From Thresholds to Therapeutic Strategies

Clinically, the 5 mm (model-derived) and site-specific critical-size concepts guide whether conservative, osteoconductive, osteoinductive, or osteogenic strategies are required. <cite id="78468f3e-2">Rodent calvarial “critical” thresholds near 5 mm underscore how healing capacity is anatomical-site–dependent and that human thresholds are not directly transferable from animal models</cite>. <cite id="78468f3e-1">Where infection coexists with segmental bone loss, criticality increases and treatment strategies (Ilizarov, Papineau, Masquelet, RIA) show wide success variability, reinforcing that biological milieu and soft-tissue viability shape outcomes</cite>. <cite id="c56c238d-0">Because defects are initially avascular, successful craniofacial bone regeneration requires integrating vasculogenesis with osteogenesis, using angiogenic factors, prevascularized or vascularized constructs, and scaffolds that guide cell behavior</cite>. <cite id="78468f3e-3">A unifying framework emphasizes scaffolds, cells/growth factors, and engineered vasculature to sustain tissue survival as constructs exceed critical size</cite>.

Practically, this translates into choosing interventions that bridge the gap between nonhealing CSBDs and functional restoration. <cite id="c56c238d-2">Autologous/allogeneic bone grafts remain gold standards but carry donor-site morbidity, infection risk, and challenges establishing deep vasculogenesis, leading to graft necrosis; new strategies target neovascular networks to improve integration</cite>. <cite id="b06d4076-0">Reconstruction must provide temporary structural support while restoring neuroprotection, mechanics for jaw motion, facial esthetics, and faster healing</cite>. <cite id="c56c238d-1">In oncologic reconstructions such as segmental mandibulectomy, microvascular composite free flaps and timely implant placement restore airway, speech, contour, and mastication, highlighting the coupling of hard- and soft-tissue healing</cite>.

Key Takeaways

- Etiologies and burden: Craniofacial bone defects from congenital, traumatic, and oncologic causes impose major functional, cosmetic, and economic burdens, demanding multidisciplinary, site-specific reconstruction. <cite id="b06d4076-0">Large craniomaxillofacial defects are often critical and require surgical reconstruction</cite>; <cite id="b06d4076-2">trauma and oncologic resection are major drivers</cite>; <cite id="b06d4076-0">annual U.S. presentations exceed 400,000 with >$1B cost</cite>; <cite id="c56c238d-0">defects impair mastication, speech, and aesthetics</cite>.
- CSBD definition and thresholds: <cite id="78468f3e-0">CSBDs are defects that won’t heal without surgery</cite>; <cite id="78468f3e-1">no universal human definition exists, though 50% cortical loss with 1 cm length has been used in tibia</cite>; <cite id="78468f3e-2">rodent calvarial ~5 mm and human calvarial >2–2.5 cm are commonly cited, but human evidence is limited and site-specific</cite>.
- Mechanisms: <cite id="c56c238d-0">Initial avascularity kills recruited osteogenic cells; regeneration needs concurrent vasculogenesis with osteogenesis</cite>; <cite id="78468f3e-3">scaffolds, cells/growth factors, and engineered vasculature are required to sustain tissue survival beyond a size threshold</cite>.
- Oncologic/functional complexity: <cite id="c56c238d-1">Segmental mandibulectomy exemplifies the need to restore airway, speech, contour, and mastication via microvascular reconstructions and dental rehabilitation</cite>; <cite id="c56c238d-4">current gold standards face limitations in replicating complex mandibular geometry and function, underscoring unmet needs</cite>.

Remaining uncertainties and clinical translation gaps include whether a precise human calvarial “5 mm” rule applies, how infection and radiation compromise criticality, and how to reliably engineer prevascularized constructs that integrate in complex craniofacial sites. <cite id="78468f3e-2">Extrapolating animal thresholds to humans is cautioned due to differences in bone architecture and regenerative capacity</cite>, and <cite id="c56c238d-2">donor-site morbidity, infection, and deep vascularization failure remain key risks of current grafts</cite>. Ongoing advances in biomaterials, prevascularized scaffolds, and combined osteogenic/angiogenic strategies aim to restore the intertwined needs for blood supply and bone continuity that define CSBD care. <cite id="c56c238d-0">Reconstruction strategies now explicitly couple osteogenesis with vasculogenesis, using angiogenic factors and cell-based vascularization, and engineering scaffold topography to direct cell behavior</cite>. <cite id="78468f3e-3">This integrative view—cells, growth factors, biomimetic structure, and engineered vasculature—frames the next wave of critical-size craniofacial bone defect repair</cite>.
</answer>

Snippet: Large bone defects affecting the craniomaxillofacial region (Figure 1) (Koller et al., 2020) can arise from high energy impact, trauma, blast injuries, congenital bone defects, and the resection of locally aggressive tumors (Keating et al., 2005). A considerable number of these defects are sufficiently large and cannot spontaneously heal on their own. These defects are "critical-sized", as they require surgical intervention and planned reconstruction to heal successfully. In all, more than 400,000 patients present to the emergency room with facial fractures or large craniofacial defects and require treatment each year, which costs over $1 billion in healthcare costs (Erdmann et al., 2008;Allareddy et al., 2011;American Society of Plastic Surgeons, 2017). Recent reports show that the incidence of craniomaxillofacial defects continues to rise by nearly 15% per year (Roden et al., 2012). Craniomaxillofacial defects, regardless of the cause, can affect function and esthetics which can be debilitating and socially incapacitating. Large-sized bone defects are also biomedically and economically burdensome (Szpalski et al., 2010). These defects require three-dimensional structural support, including permanent protection of the underlying brain tissue, mechanical integrity, allowance for the full range of jaw movement, and excellent facial esthetics along with faster healing rates.

Title: The Role of Skeletal Stem Cells in the Reconstruction of Bone Defects
Snippet: Abstract Craniofacial surgery, since its inauguration, has been the culmination of collaborative efforts to solve complex congenital, dysplastic, oncological, and traumatic cranial bone defects. Now, 50 years on from the first craniofacial meeting, the collaborative efforts between surgeons, scientists, and bioengineers are further advancing craniofacial surgery with new discoveries in tissue regeneration. Recent advances in regenerative medicine and stem cell biology have transformed the authors’ understanding of bone healing, the role of stem cells governing bone healing, and the effects of the niche environment and extracellular matrix on stem cell fate. This review aims at summarizing the advances within each of these fields.

Title: The current regenerative medicine approaches of craniofacial diseases: A narrative review
Snippet: Traumatic or oncological resection or congenital abnormalities can cause craniofacial defects (CFDs). A non-healing composite tissue wound is caused by soft tissue deficits, bone loss, or both. Treatment of craniofacial defects is difficult because there are many different types of tissues and structures (Nyberg et al., 2017). Maxillofacial (MF) fractures result from many factors, such as crashes in motor fights, firearms, vehicles, wars, and sports (Herford, 2017;Castro-Espicalsky et al., 2020). Those with musculoskeletal dysfunctions usually suffer significant negative effects from CFDs (Martín-Del-Campo et al., 2019). Iran had to provide prolonged medical care to over 400 thousand patients due to the Iraq-Iran war. Official organizations authorized to assist war victims invited international reconstruction surgeons to Iran. The leader of this team was Paul Tessier, the founder of craniofacial surgery. During this project, patients with severe trauma injuries in the lower part of the face were provided with MF and oral rehabilitation using the most current techniques (Simon et al., 2015). There are differences in the incidence rates of trauma according to countries worldwide. Trauma is one of the top five factors contributing to death worldwide (Herford, 2017). United States children suffer from it more often than any other disease. Based on the National Trauma Databank collected, pediatric trauma cases most commonly involve the head, with the face being the fourth most common body part to be injured. Case fatality rates of 3.74% and 3.07% were reported for pediatric head and face injuries in 2016 (Braun et al., 2017). The burden of oral diseases is heavily influenced by periodontal disease (Latimer et al., 2021). According to the World Health Organization (WHO), the number of people affected by this high-impact disease grew by 6% from 2017 to 2018 (Global and regional, 2018).

Title: Pediatric Maxillofacial Fractures: Patterns of Injury, Surgical Indications, and Treatment Outcomes: A Five-Year Retrospective Study
Snippet: Pediatric craniofacial fractures represent a distinct clinical entity that differs substantially from adult facial trauma with respect to epidemiology, biomechanics, diagnostic challenges, and therapeutic principles. Although relatively uncommon-accounting for approximately 1% to 15% of all facial fractures-these injuries demand particular clinical attention due to their potential to result in long-term functional impairment, facial asymmetry, growth disturbances, and psychosocial sequelae if inadequately treated [1]. 

The lower incidence of facial fractures in children compared with adults can be attributed to unique anatomical and physiological characteristics, including a larger craniumto-face ratio, greater elasticity of the facial skeleton, and thicker adipose and soft tissue coverage. Collectively, these features provide a degree of natural protection against fracture propagation [2]. Nevertheless, when fractures do occur, their management is often more complex than in adults, primarily because of the presence of active craniofacial growth centers, developing dentition, and varying bone remodeling capacities [3]. Pediatric facial bones contain a higher proportion of cancellous bone and demonstrate greater osteogenic potential, facilitating rapid healing but also predisposing to growth abnormalities if treatment is poorly timed or improperly executed [4]. 

Consequently, treatment protocols developed for adults cannot be directly applied to pediatric patients. Clinical decision-making must carefully balance the goals of anatomical reduction and stable fixation with the preservation of facial growth potential and normal functional development [5]. 

The etiology of pediatric facial fractures is strongly age-dependent. In younger children, falls and domestic accidents predominate, whereas in school-aged children and adolescents, road traffic collisions and sports-related injuries are more frequent [6]. Importantly, pediatric facial fractures are often associated with concomitant injuries, particularly to the central nervous system, cervical spine, and thoracoabdominal region. This underscores the importance of comprehensive trauma evaluation and multidisciplinary management involving pediatric surgeons, maxillofacial specialists, and neurosurgeons [7]. 

Despite increasing interest in pediatric craniofacial trauma, the current body of evidence on the epidemiology, management, and long-term outcomes of pediatric facial fractures remains heterogeneous.

documents.snippet: Large bone defects affecting the craniomaxillofacial region (Figure 1) (Koller et al., 2020) can arise from high energy impact, trauma, blast injuries, congenital bone defects, and the resection of locally aggressive tumors (Keating et al., 2005). A considerable number of these defects are sufficiently large and cannot spontaneously heal on their own. These defects are "critical-sized", as they require surgical intervention and planned reconstruction to heal successfully. In all, more than 400,000 patients present to the emergency room with facial fractures or large craniofacial defects and require treatment each year, which costs over $1 billion in healthcare costs (Erdmann et al., 2008;Allareddy et al., 2011;American Society of Plastic Surgeons, 2017). Recent reports show that the incidence of craniomaxillofacial defects continues to rise by nearly 15% per year (Roden et al., 2012). Craniomaxillofacial defects, regardless of the cause, can affect function and esthetics which can be debilitating and socially incapacitating. Large-sized bone defects are also biomedically and economically burdensome (Szpalski et al., 2010). These defects require three-dimensional structural support, including permanent protection of the underlying brain tissue, mechanical integrity, allowance for the full range of jaw movement, and excellent facial esthetics along with faster healing rates.

documents.snippet:
Pediatric craniofacial fractures represent a distinct clinical entity that differs substantially from adult facial trauma with respect to epidemiology, biomechanics, diagnostic challenges, and therapeutic principles. Although relatively uncommon-accounting for approximately 1% to 15% of all facial fractures-these injuries demand particular clinical attention due to their potential to result in long-term functional impairment, facial asymmetry, growth disturbances, and psychosocial sequelae if inadequately treated [1]. 

The lower incidence of facial fractures in children compared with adults can be attributed to unique anatomical and physiological characteristics, including a larger craniumto-face ratio, greater elasticity of the facial skeleton, and thicker adipose and soft tissue coverage. Collectively, these features provide a degree of natural protection against fracture propagation [2]. Nevertheless, when fractures do occur, their management is often more complex than in adults, primarily because of the presence of active craniofacial growth centers, developing dentition, and varying bone remodeling capacities [3]. Pediatric facial bones contain a higher proportion of cancellous bone and demonstrate greater osteogenic potential, facilitating rapid healing but also predisposing to growth abnormalities if treatment is poorly timed or improperly executed [4]. 

Consequently, treatment protocols developed for adults cannot be directly applied to pediatric patients. Clinical decision-making must carefully balance the goals of anatomical reduction and stable fixation with the preservation of facial growth potential and normal functional development [5]. 

The etiology of pediatric facial fractures is strongly age-dependent. In younger children, falls and domestic accidents predominate, whereas in school-aged children and adolescents, road traffic collisions and sports-related injuries are more frequent [6]. Importantly, pediatric facial fractures are often associated with concomitant injuries, particularly to the central nervous system, cervical spine, and thoracoabdominal region. This underscores the importance of comprehensive trauma evaluation and multidisciplinary management involving pediatric surgeons, maxillofacial specialists, and neurosurgeons [7]. 

Despite increasing interest in pediatric craniofacial trauma, the current body of evidence on the epidemiology, management, and long-term outcomes of pediatric facial fractures remains heterogeneous.

Title: Management of critical-sized bone defects in the treatment of fracture-related infection: a systematic review and pooled analysis
Snippet: Segmental bone loss after trauma remains a challenging problem for orthopedic trauma surgeons. When a bone defect exists combined with fracture-related infection (FRI), the chances of successful bone consolidation and clearance of infection are reduced. 

A 'critical-sized' defect is a bone defect which is not expected to heal in the absence of a secondary (surgical) intervention. There is no agreed definition of what constitutes a critical defect in humans. Court-Brown defined it [1] as a defect involving 50% of the cortical diameter with a minimum length of 1 cm, and this was used in the Study to Prospectively evaluate Intramedullary Nails in Tibial fractures (SPRINT) [2]. A study by Sanders et al. [3] showed that, when using this definition, 47% of the bone defects healed without additional surgery, thus indicating that these are not always critical defects. When infection is present, it is much less likely that the fracture will heal [4,5], so in this analysis, The SPRINT definition for a critical-sized defect in FRI was accepted. 

Over the past decades, critical-sized bone defects in FRI have been treated using different protocols. Techniques used (e.g., Ilizarov, Papineau, Masquelet, or RIA) all have different indications and success rates, resulting in a wide range of clinical outcomes. The aim of this systematic review and pooled analysis was to evaluate identified treatment strategies, their individual success rates and other outcome parameters regarding critical-sized bone defects used between 1990 and 2018.

Snippet: Periosteal vascular network damage has been shown to significantly decrease the healing potential and may require the use of vascularized reconstruction techniques [29,38,39]. 

The concept of critical-size defects (CSDs) is a fundamental issue related to cranial bone repair and regeneration. Schmitz and Hollinger initially defined it as the smallest intraosseous wound in a particular bone and species of animal that will not heal spontaneously during its lifetime [30]. Currently, it is understood as a cranial defect that cannot be healed without surgical intervention, with a variable size depending on the anatomical location and individual patient-related factors. A recent meta-analysis on rodent models suggested that a calvarial defect exceeding 5.0 mm should be considered a CSD; however, the heterogeneity of the included studies was high [40]. In dogs, 20.0 mm was considered the critical threshold [30]. In humans, there is no clearly defined CSD value, as a study to properly evaluate it would likely breach numerous ethical recommendations. In addition, extrapolation from animal models is not recommended, as the bone structure and capacity for bone regeneration differ significantly [41]. Although a human calvarial defect exceeding 2-2.5 cm is considered incapable of spontaneous healing, these values have not been proven through a high-level scientific approach [42][43][44]. The unique anatomical features of the cranial bone structure present specific challenges for regenerative approaches, which differ significantly from long bone repair. The human cranium contains 22 bones, divided primarily into two main regions: the neurocranium, which protects the brain and sensory organs, and the viscerocranium, which supports the facial structure. This complex architecture encompasses bones with distinct developmental origins, healing characteristics, vascularization, thicknesses, and ratios of cortical versus porous bone, among other features [45]. Cranial bone formation is driven by two distinct ossification processes. The cranial base is primarily formed through endochondral ossification, resulting in a more compact, dense, and less flexible structure.

Snippet: The definition of a critical size bone defect is the smallest possible defect in bone that will not heal during the lifetime of an organism. For many models, the term critical size bone defect is accepted although it may not be clear whether or not the defect is of the smallest in size. Additionally, the end of an experiment is often determined by the endpoint rather than by the natural lifespan of an organism [8]. 

The choice of a relevant animal model is vital in the development of bone implants. There is a wide range of animals used for investigating different aspects of bone healing and the integration of tissue engineered implants. Desired properties of a model are reproducibility and the chance to conduct different analysis, while morbidity as well as mortality of the animal should be as low as possible until the end of the experiment. 

A common view on bone tissue engineering portrays four vital aspects for bone regeneration. A scaffold that is similar in composition and structure to the natural extracellular environment of the bone. Cells are able to produce new bone matrix and additionally, growth factors that facilitate cell differentiation or attract desirable cell types including blood vessels and finally, a vasculature in order to support cell survival for tissues exceeding a certain size [9]. 

The advances and current developments of vascularization which is necessary to support the survival of cell-seeded implants that exceed a certain size will be reviewed and discussed in the context of bone regeneration.

Title: Vascularization Reconstruction Strategies in Craniofacial Bone Regeneration
Snippet: Craniofacial bone defects are usually secondary to accident trauma, resection of tumor, sever inflammation, and congenital disease. The defects of craniofacial bones impact esthetic appearance and functionality such as mastication, pronunciation, and facial features. During the craniofacial bone regeneration process, different osteogenic cells are introduced, including primary osteoblasts or pluripotent stem cells. However, the defect area is initially avascular, resulting in the death of the introduced cells and failed regeneration. Thus, it is vital to establish vascularization strategies to build a timely and abundant blood vessel supply network. This review paper therefore focuses on the reconstruction of both osteogenesis and vasculogenesis. The current challenges, various strategies, and latest efforts applied to enhance vascularization in craniofacial bone regeneration are discussed. These involve the application of angiogenic growth factors and cell-based vascularization strategies. In addition, surface morphology, porous characters, and the angiogenic release property of scaffolds also have a fundamental effect on vasculogenesis via cell behavior and are further discussed.

Title: Mandibular rehabilitation: From the Andy Gump deformity to jaw‐in‐a‐day
Snippet: The mandible is a critical structure of the lower facial skeleton which plays an important role in several vital functions, including feeding, speech production and breathing. Segmental resection of the mandible is at times required to ensure en bloc tumor removal in patients with advanced oral cavity malignancies. It is less commonly performed for primary tumors of the mandible or for osteonecrosis related to radiation therapy or bisphosphonates. 2][3][4][5] Mandibular reconstruction is warranted to restore airway patency, improve speech articulation, reestablish the lower facial contour, and restore adequate oral intake. 

The latter is particularly challenging given the complex threedimensional anatomy of the mandible. 7][8] Significant advances have been made over the past decade in the ability to reconstruct and rehabilitate patients after a segmental mandibulectomy. This includes composite microvascular free tissue transfer, as well as dental restoration. This review will highlight these advances, evaluate their efficacy, and discuss the timing of dental implantation.

Title: Vascularization Reconstruction Strategies in Craniofacial Bone Regeneration
Snippet: Craniofacial bone provides support for adjacent craniofacial soft tissues (especially the attachments of mastication-related muscles) and anchorage for dental structures [1]. The defects of craniofacial bones, secondary to accident trauma, congenital disease, tumor resection, and inflammation [2][3][4][5], impact esthetic appearance and functionality of the craniofacial complex, such as mastication, pronunciation, and facial features. Furthermore, craniofacial bone is highly vascularized, and its functions depend a lot on an unobstructed and well-organized vascular network. With the intact vessels, sufficient oxygen and nutrients can be supplied, guaranteeing the proliferation and viability of cells [6]. At the same time, the metabolic waste of cells can be taken away [7]. Therefore, it is wellrecognized that the prompting of vasculogenesis is beneficial for reinforced bone functions. After the craniofacial bone defect occurs, osteogenic cells such as primary osteoblasts or pluripotent stem cells are recruited in order to generate neobones. However, the defect area is initially avascular, resulting in the death of the recruited cells and failed regeneration [6]. Thus, it is vital to establish vascularization strategies to build a timely and abundant blood vessel supply network [8]. 

Clinically, the damaged craniofacial bone can be reconstructed with a series of surgical operations. More than 90% of grafts used are autologous or allogenic transplantations, which are recognized as the "gold standards" [9]. However, challenges, such as donor site morbidity, pain, infection, and additional economic burden, are still unmet [10]. More importantly, vasculogenesis in the depth of the defect also cannot be well-established, which leads to the necrosis of transplanted grafts [11][12][13]. 

Coatings 2024, 14, 357 2 of 18 Rapid developments in bone tissue engineering bring new hope for solving the urgent problems and provide more strategies for neovascular networks and craniofacial bone tissue regeneration.

Title: Reconstructive strategies for post-oncological oral and maxillofacial defects: A systematic overview of novel techniques and outcomes
Snippet: Oral and maxillofacial defects caused by resection of tumors are extremely frequently complicated post-oncology defects and affect the strategies of reconstruction. These defects are classified according to their localization in the human body (oral cavity, mandible, maxilla and midface) and lesion of anatomical structure: (a) soft-tissue, (b) hardtissue or (c) composite. Correctly classifying lesions, e.g., the brown system of classifying maxillary defects, enlightens the approach to surgery, considering the functions (speech and swallowing) and aesthetics. Defining the nature of defects is crucial for selecting the most effective method of reconstruction, as it also improves patient outcomes.

Title: The Potential of Magnesium Based Materials in Mandibular Reconstruction
Snippet: The mandible is the largest and the strongest bone in the human face, serving as a support to the oral musculature and thereby aiding in articulation, respiration, deglutition, and mastication. Furthermore, it is crucial in maintaining the facial profile by supporting the skeletal base for teeth [1]. Several issues like tumor resection, congenital defects, and associated trauma needing many reconstructive surgeries in the mandibular zone is one of the routine challenges in clinical practice [2]. One of the potential challenges often encountered by clinicians is the oromandibular reconstruction during episodes of benign/malignant tumor resection, and management of osteomyelitis or the osteoradionecrotic mandible. Mandibular defects often occur due to the surgical therapies for malignant tumors surfacing in the neck and head regions. Often, these defects jeopardize both form and function of the mandible, requiring a multi-disciplinary approach to restore their function and aesthetics. Significant factors to be considered during the reconstruction of such defects include the re-establishment of facial dimensions in terms of their width, height, and projection. Despite the advancements, during the critical assessment of the reconstructed oral cavity, functional deficits are often encountered. Besides radical removal of the tumor, current prospects of maxillofacial surgery demand subsequent primary/secondary reconstruction taking into consideration the patient factors that have an important role in terms of efficient function, aesthetics, and dental rehabilitation. Various surgical methodologies have been adopted for mandibular defect reconstruction that possess unique advantages and limitations. Some of these surgical procedures include free bone graft, reconstruction plate, particulate bone cancellous marrow graft, transport distraction osteogenesis, microvascular free flap, pedicle bone graft, modular endoprosthesis, and tissue engineering. 

The current gold standard treatment modalities for mandibular defect reconstruction includes: (a) vascularized microvascular free fibula flap or (b) an autogenous free bone graft. However, the bone graft treatment possesses certain limitations, such as its inability to replicate the complex geometry of the original mandible. Further, it also lacks in mimicking the aesthetic and function aspect completely like the original.

Segmental resection of the mandible is at times required to ensure en bloc tumor removal in patients with advanced oral cavity malignancies. It is less commonly performed for primary tumors of the mandible or for osteonecrosis related to radiation therapy or bisphosphonates. 2][3][4][5] Mandibular reconstruction is warranted to restore airway patency, improve speech articulation, reestablish the lower facial contour, and restore adequate oral intake. 

The latter is particularly challenging given the complex threedimensional anatomy of the mandible. 7][8] Significant advances have been made over the past decade in the ability to reconstruct and rehabilitate patients after a segmental mandibulectomy. This includes composite microvascular free tissue transfer, as well as dental restoration. This review will highlight these advances, evaluate their efficacy, and discuss the timing of dental implantation.

snippet.text:
Craniofacial bone provides support for adjacent craniofacial soft tissues (especially the attachments of mastication-related muscles) and anchorage for dental structures [1]. The defects of craniofacial bones, secondary to accident trauma, congenital disease, tumor resection, and inflammation [2][3][4][5], impact esthetic appearance and functionality of the craniofacial complex, such as mastication, pronunciation, and facial features. Furthermore, craniofacial bone is highly vascularized, and its functions depend a lot on an unobstructed and well-organized vascular network. With the intact vessels, sufficient oxygen and nutrients can be supplied, guaranteeing the proliferation and viability of cells [6]. At the same time, the metabolic waste of cells can be taken away [7]. Therefore, it is wellrecognized that the prompting of vasculogenesis is beneficial for reinforced bone functions. After the craniofacial bone defect occurs, osteogenic cells such as primary osteoblasts or pluripotent stem cells are recruited in order to generate neobones. However, the defect area is initially avascular, resulting in the death of the recruited cells and failed regeneration [6]. Thus, it is vital to establish vascularization strategies to build a timely and abundant blood vessel supply network [8]. 

Clinically, the damaged craniofacial bone can be reconstructed with a series of surgical operations. More than 90% of grafts used are autologous or allogenic transplantations, which are recognized as the "gold standards" [9]. However, challenges, such as donor site morbidity, pain, infection, and additional economic burden, are still unmet [10]. More importantly, vasculogenesis in the depth of the defect also cannot be well-established, which leads to the necrosis of transplanted grafts [11][12][13]. 

Coatings 2024, 14, 357 2 of 18 Rapid developments in bone tissue engineering bring new hope for solving the urgent problems and provide more strategies for neovascular networks and craniofacial bone tissue regeneration.

snippet.text: Oral and maxillofacial defects caused by resection of tumors are extremely frequently complicated post-oncology defects and affect the strategies of reconstruction. These defects are classified according to their localization in the human body (oral cavity, mandible, maxilla and midface) and lesion of anatomical structure: (a) soft-tissue, (b) hardtissue or (c) composite. Correctly classifying lesions, e.g., the brown system of classifying maxillary defects, enlightens the approach to surgery, considering the functions (speech and swallowing) and aesthetics. Defining the nature of defects is crucial for selecting the most effective method of reconstruction, as it also improves patient outcomes.

snippet.text:
The mandible is the largest and the strongest bone in the human face, serving as a support to the oral musculature and thereby aiding in articulation, respiration, deglutition, and mastication. Furthermore, it is crucial in maintaining the facial profile by supporting the skeletal base for teeth [1]. Several issues like tumor resection, congenital defects, and associated trauma needing many reconstructive surgeries in the mandibular zone is one of the routine challenges in clinical practice [2]. One of the potential challenges often encountered by clinicians is the oromandibular reconstruction during episodes of benign/malignant tumor resection, and management of osteomyelitis or the osteoradionecrotic mandible. Mandibular defects often occur due to the surgical therapies for malignant tumors surfacing in the neck and head regions. Often, these defects jeopardize both form and function of the mandible, requiring a multi-disciplinary approach to restore their function and aesthetics. Significant factors to be considered during the reconstruction of such defects include the re-establishment of facial dimensions in terms of their width, height, and projection. Despite the advancements, during the critical assessment of the reconstructed oral cavity, functional deficits are often encountered. Besides radical removal of the tumor, current prospects of maxillofacial surgery demand subsequent primary/secondary reconstruction taking into consideration the patient factors that have an important role in terms of efficient function, aesthetics, and dental rehabilitation. Various surgical methodologies have been adopted for mandibular defect reconstruction that possess unique advantages and limitations. Some of these surgical procedures include free bone graft, reconstruction plate, particulate bone cancellous marrow graft, transport distraction osteogenesis, microvascular free flap, pedicle bone graft, modular endoprosthesis, and tissue engineering. 

The current gold standard treatment modalities for mandibular defect reconstruction includes: (a) vascularized microvascular free fibula flap or (b) an autogenous free bone graft. However, the bone graft treatment possesses certain limitations, such as its inability to replicate the complex geometry of the original mandible. Further, it also lacks in mimicking the aesthetic and function aspect completely like the original.

attempts.answer:
Summary
A “5 mm” critical-size threshold for craniofacial bone defect healing is most firmly supported for calvarium in rodent models, but across the craniofacial skeleton—including the maxilla, mandible, and orbital floor—the actual critical size is anatomical- and species-specific and modulated by local biology and mechanics. Consequently, 5 mm can be used as a screening breakpoint for calvarial defects, but smaller defects may also fail to heal in some sites (e.g., certain maxillary contexts), while the orbital floor often heals via fibrous bridging at even smaller dimensions, especially with membrane augmentation. <cite id="ca9c6e16-4">Critical-size defects are defined as the smallest intraosseous wounds in a particular bone and species that do not heal spontaneously; human critical sizes are undefined and vary with site and patient factors</cite><cite id="ca9c6e16-4">A meta-analysis in rodent calvarial models suggested 5.0 mm as a critical threshold but with high heterogeneity, while larger animals showed higher thresholds (e.g., 20 mm in dogs) and human extrapolation is not recommended</cite>.

Definitions and Principles
- Critical-size defect (CSD) denotes the minimal defect that fails to heal via the body’s native bridging capacity, instead forming fibrous tissue; below this size, endochondral or intramembranous bone formation spans the gap without intervention. <cite id="be65e608-3">A bone defect is categorized as critical size when the native tissue cannot bridge the gap and fibrotic tissue is deposited; below this size healing can restore the defect, while at or above CSD intervention is required</cite>.
- The same total linear dimension can map to very different areas and stress environments across sites (e.g., 5 mm diameter is 19.6 mm² on convex calvarium but much smaller on the concave orbital floor), so area, edge stability, and soft-tissue cover matter as much as the measured dimension. <cite id="ca9c6e16-4">Cranial bone varies widely in vascularization, cortical/porous composition, and healing characteristics across neurocranium and viscerocranium, making thresholds variable</cite>.

Calvarium (skullcap)
- Origin of the 5 mm rule: rodent calvarial studies using intramembranous bone formation show that defects beyond about 5 mm generally fail to bridge without grafting or osteoinductive cues, motivating a pragmatic 5 mm breakpoint in screening. <cite id="ca9c6e16-4">A recent meta-analysis on rodent models suggested that a calvarial defect exceeding 5.0 mm should be considered a CSD, though heterogeneity is high</cite>.
- Biological context: calvarium heals largely by direct intramembranous ossification with dural-derived osteogenic cells and a comparatively permissive vascular niche; this supports lower thresholds and explains why calvarial bone from this site (and split-thickness calvarial grafts) resorbs less than endochondral grafts and is favored in craniofacial reconstructions. <cite id="ca9c6e16-0">Calvarial bone grafts undergo less resorption than endochondral sources and are minimally morbid; dura loses its capacity for calvarial reossification after age two</cite>.
- Caveats: Even in rodents, “critical size” is model-dependent; defect geometry, trephine size, edge stability, and evaluation windows vary across studies, and human translation remains uncertain. <cite id="ca9c6e16-1">In a standardized rat maxillary model, 2.8–4.5 mm circular defects showed incomplete mineralization and no complete healing by 12 weeks, illustrating that critical thresholds are not universally 5 mm</cite><cite id="ca9c6e16-4">Heterogeneity in calvarial CSD thresholds is high across studies, and extrapolation from animals to humans is not recommended due to structural and regenerative differences</cite>.

Maxilla
- Evidence from rat maxillary alveolar bone defects indicates that circular defects as small as 2.8–3.3–4.5 mm, when stably positioned between an incisor and palatine suture, may still fail to achieve complete bridging by 12 weeks, with bone volume/defect fill below 40% and little further increase beyond six weeks; the smallest 2.8 mm defect was selected as operationally feasible but not necessarily healing. <cite id="ca9c6e16-1">At 12 weeks, 2.8–4.5 mm maxillary defects in rats showed incomplete mineralization and no complete healing; complete healing was not observed, and the 2.8 mm defect was chosen as the smallest feasible size</cite>.
- Mechanistic modifiers: the maxilla combines relatively low osteogenic turnover at baseline with the presence of the periodontal ligament space and proximity to the sinus, which can impede intramembranous bridging and promote fibrosis if the defect is too narrow or unsupported; stabilization and augmentation strategies are often required in such models. <cite id="be65e608-0">The mandible (and by analogy the maxilla) is under cyclic loading; site-specific healing mechanisms and progenitors likely differ from calvaria, and models that simulate loading change expected outcomes</cite><cite id="ca9c6e16-1">Maxillary defects in this model did not reach 40% bone volume fill by 12 weeks and showed incomplete healing, highlighting the need for intervention</cite>.
- Cross-site comparison: while calvarial CSDs are often cited around 5 mm in rodents, maxillary CSDs in small animals may occur at smaller linear sizes when the defect disrupts periodontal homeostasis or lacks hard-bone edge support, underscoring that 5 mm is not universally “critical” for the maxilla. <cite id="ca9c6e16-4">Calvarial CSDs around 5 mm are suggested in rodents, but thresholds vary by bone and species; the maxilla’s distinct vascularization and healing characteristics imply different practical CSDs</cite><cite id="ca9c6e16-1">Maxillary 2.8–4.5 mm defects in rats did not heal fully by 12 weeks, indicating smaller critical sizes in this context</cite>.

Mandible
- Direct experimental evidence in rats shows a 5 mm segmental defect in the mandible does not heal into bony union within 12 weeks, whereas 0–1–3 mm defects do bridge, establishing 5 mm as that species’ critical-size breakpoint under internal fixation; the mechanical environment of mastication and periosteal biology likely drive the higher mandibular threshold compared with calvaria. <cite id="be65e608-4">In a rat model, 5-mm segmental mandibular defects did not heal, while 0-, 1-, and 3-mm defects did, with significantly lower bone union scores for 5-mm defects; thus, 5 mm defines the rat segmental mandibular CSD</cite>.
- Mechanistic context: the mandible experiences continuous functional loading and relies on periosteal and endosteal progenitors with the periodontal ligament anchoring constraints; pilot and comparative models indicate that scaling defect size to 5 mm can exceed the self-healing capacity, and that fully stabilized models may understate the impact of physiologic loading on healing dynamics. <cite id="be65e608-0">Mandibular models subjected to functional loading heal via mechanisms distinct from calvaria; the rate and quality of healing are influenced by location-specific progenitors and mechanics</cite><cite id="be65e608-0">A 2.3 mm defect that did not spontaneously heal after 8 weeks in an angular process model illustrates that small defects can be CSD under certain conditions, but scaling and injury to adjacent structures (e.g., masseter) affect outcomes</cite>.

Title: Induction of Mandibular Cortical Bone Defects to Study Bone Regeneration
Snippet: To date, a method for generation of defects within the mandible body in the absence of endochondral bone formation has not described. Other groups reported induction of a 2.3 mm defect that represented a critical sized defect that did not spontaneously heal after 8 weeks, but this model also required injury of the masseter and was placed within the angular process of the mandible [26]. Although calvarial defects are commonly used to study intramembranous regeneration in the craniofacial skeleton, development of the model described within this manuscript will aid in studying site-specific healing. Unlike the calvaria, the mandible is subjected to cyclic mechanical loading resulting from mastication. Moreover, site-specific mechanisms of skeletal healing, including location specific progenitors, may greatly enhance our understanding of musculoskeletal regeneration [3,[27][28][29]. 

We did not generate a critical sized defect within this pilot study, as our goal was to establish a model of bone healing within the mandible that is amenable to studying how interventions (e.g., cellular, genetic, therapeutics) may modulate healing within the mandible. It may be possible to scale the defect size using the method described within this manuscript to achieve a critical sized defect that does not spontaneously heal. 

While single cortex defect models are useful for understanding the basic cellular processes in bone repair, these models have limitations. The rate of skeletal healing is likely accelerated as compared to a fracture. Although little bone formation is expected three days post-defect generation, we were not sufficiently powered to observe differences in healing between days 0 and 3 versus later time points within this pilot study. While the defects generated using this method are reproducible, they do not reflect a true fracture of the mandible; thus, reduced inflammatory and immune responses and lack of endosteal marrow components are limitations of this model. Likewise, the effects of mechanical loading of the mandible may be minimized within this fully stabilized model.

Snippet: Mandibular defects may arise from a variety of etiologies, including congenital conditions, malignant or benign tumor resection, osteoradionecrosis, osteomyelitis, and trauma [1]. The size of the defect is extremely impactful in the healing process and determines whether medical intervention is necessary. A bone defect is categorized as critical size when the native tissue is unable to bridge the gap between the remaining bone, and fibrotic tissue is deposited instead of mineralized bone tissue [2]. Below this critical defect size, the body's inherent physiological healing processes can restore the damage, and therefore little to no medical intervention is required [3]. However, critical size defects necessitate medical intervention in order to enable healing. 

The mandible is the single largest craniofacial bone and therefore plays a vital role in both function and aesthetics of the head and neck region. Functions including mastication, speech, swallowing, and airway accessibility all can be impacted as a result of mandibular defects. This not only decreases the quality of life for patients but also in more severe cases may increase morbidity and mortality [1,4]. Additionally, people living with a craniofacial deformity can experience social stigma and psychological stress, such as depression and anxiety. 

Given the significant impact of mandibular defects on a patient's daily functions and quality of life, surgeons and engineers have worked together to develop reconstruction techniques.
